patient.name: Zainab Rahman
patient.setting: Sexual health clinic, then antenatal clinic
patient.complaint: Painful genital sores and burning on passing urine for 3 days; 35 weeks pregnant
background: First pregnancy, 35 weeks, uncomplicated so far
Never had cold sores or genital sores before
Partner gets cold sores; recent oral sex
Works as a pharmacist in Tower Hamlets; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with painful grouped vesicles or ulcers after a tingling prodrome, against painless syphilis; plus questions on keratitis (dendritic ulcer), erythema multiforme, encephalitis and neonatal herpes.

points: Two days of **tingling and burning** in the vulva, then sores appeared.

steps.lead: Painful vesicles on mucosa point to **HSV**. Her partner's cold sores are **HSV-1**, which can cause genital disease too.
Zainab's risk is **sexual contact**; pregnancy also mildly suppresses immunity.

points: Exam: **grouped vesicles on a red base** on both labia.
Some have burst into shallow, very **painful ulcers**.

steps.lead: Zainab has the full picture: **prodrome**, grouped vesicles becoming painful ulcers, **lymphadenopathy** and **dysuria**.

steps.q: Zainab has painful grouped vesicles and ulcers after a tingling prodrome. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: **Painful grouped vesicles** after a prodrome = genital herpes. Syphilis is painless; warts are painless growths.

visual.title: Recurrent herpes: how often is there a prodrome?
visual.label: about 50%
visual.caption: About **half** of recurrences give a tingling warning. Zainab is told to **abstain from sex** until the prodrome and lesions fully resolve.

steps.lead: HSV can also hit the eye (**dendritic ulcer**), trigger **erythema multiforme**, or infect Zainab's baby if she has a primary infection within **6 weeks** of birth.
For Zainab, the big worry is **neonatal herpes**. Keratitis and rare **herpes encephalitis** are the other complications to know.

steps.text: A **painless** genital ulcer is syphilis until proven otherwise. Herpes ulcers are **painful**.
HSV-1 = classically cold sores, HSV-2 = classically genital, but **either type can cause disease at either site** (oral sex spreads HSV-1 to the genitals).

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' with **HSV PCR (NAAT) on a lesion swab** as the answer, or a typical cold sore where no test is needed.

steps.lead: Zainab's grouped vesicles are classic, so the diagnosis is made **clinically** and treatment starts today.

points: Because she is pregnant, typing matters for her birth plan.
A swab is rubbed firmly over the base of an ulcer.
Sent for HSV PCR; syphilis and HIV tests are offered.

steps.lead: The swab goes for **NAAT/PCR**, the most effective test, confirming HSV and its type.

steps.q: Which test best confirms HSV from Zainab's ulcer?
o: HSV PCR on a lesion swab
steps.r: **PCR (NAAT) on a lesion swab** is the most effective test. Dark-ground microscopy is for syphilis; serology does not prove the lesion is herpes.

steps.title: Zainab's results
steps.text: Genital **HSV-1**, from her partner's cold sores via oral sex. No HSV antibodies before: a **primary** infection.

steps.title: Testing a suspected herpes lesion
nodes: Ambiguous, recurrent or pregnant: swab the lesion

steps.text: Do not wait for the PCR before starting aciclovir. Typical lesions are treated on **clinical** grounds.
Gold standard = **PCR on a lesion swab**. First-line = **clinical**. Learn both, because the lead-in tells you which one they want.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' with oral aciclovir for genital or oral herpes, topical aciclovir (no steroids) for keratitis, and elective caesarean for primary genital herpes within 6 weeks of delivery.

steps.lead: Zainab starts **oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days**, with paracetamol, hygiene advice and no sex until healed.

visual.title: Zainab on oral aciclovir
visual.caption: Pain and lesions settle over a week. Aciclovir shortens the episode but **does not clear latent virus**.

visual.title: When did Zainab's primary infection start?
bands: within 6 weeks of birth: plan caesarean
visual.label: Zainab 35 weeks
visual.caption: A primary episode within **6 weeks** of delivery carries the highest neonatal risk.

steps.lead: Zainab's primary episode is within 6 weeks of birth: **oral aciclovir** plus an **elective caesarean**. If she declines, **intrapartum IV aciclovir**.

steps.q: Zainab declines a caesarean section. Which is the most appropriate alternative?
steps.r: If caesarean is declined, give **intrapartum IV aciclovir** to reduce the risk of neonatal transmission.

points: Three weeks later Zainab rubs her eye; it becomes **red, painful and watery**.
Light hurts and vision is blurred.

steps.lead: Zainab's **herpes simplex keratitis** needs **topical aciclovir** and urgent eye review. **No topical steroid** drops.
Zainab's care follows the **BASHH genital herpes** guideline and **NICE CKS** for oral and genital herpes.

steps.text: Never give **topical steroids** for a red eye until a dendritic ulcer is excluded. Steroids can make HSV keratitis much worse.
Oral or genital herpes = **oral aciclovir 400 mg TDS, 5 days**. Valaciclovir or famciclovir are alternatives.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on latency (trigeminal ganglion for HSV-1, sacral ganglia for HSV-2), reactivation triggers, why vesicles form, why encephalitis hits the temporal lobes, or why caesarean protects the baby.

steps.lead: Zainab's HSV now hides **latent** in her **sacral ganglia**. Stress, illness or UV can reactivate it, so recurrences are likely.

steps.title: Latency and reactivation
nodes: Primary infection of skin or mucosa
Virus travels up the sensory nerve
Virus travels back down: recurrent lesions

steps.lead: Zainab's blisters formed because infected **keratinocytes swell and degenerate**, splitting the epidermis. When they burst, painful ulcers remain.

steps.q: Where does the virus lie latent after Zainab's genital infection?
steps.r: Genital HSV becomes latent in the **sacral ganglia**; oral HSV-1 in the **trigeminal ganglion**.

steps.lead: If HSV reached Zainab's brain, it would favour the **temporal lobes**, spreading along olfactory and trigeminal tracts.
If Zainab later developed target lesions on her hands after a recurrence, that is **erythema multiforme**: a hypersensitivity reaction to HSV antigens.
Zainab's caesarean stops her baby touching **infected genital secretions** in the birth canal.

steps.text: HSV is a **double-stranded DNA virus**. Latency explains why antivirals treat episodes but never cure.

mcq.q: Which HSV type classically causes cold sores?
mcq.r: **HSV-1** classically oral; **HSV-2** classically genital; either can affect either site.

mcq.q: What do herpes lesions classically look like?
o: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
mcq.r: **Grouped vesicles on a red base** that rupture into painful ulcers.

mcq.q: What is seen on fluorescein staining in HSV keratitis?
What lesion is the hallmark of erythema multiforme?
o: Target lesions with three concentric rings
mcq.r: **Target lesions with three rings**, typically on the hands and feet; HSV-1 is the commonest trigger.

mcq.q: What is the most effective test to confirm HSV?
o: HSV PCR (NAAT) on a lesion swab

mcq.q: How is a typical cold sore usually diagnosed?
What is the first-line oral treatment for genital herpes?
mcq.r: **Oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days**.

mcq.q: What must be avoided in herpes simplex keratitis?
mcq.r: **Topical steroids** can worsen the ulcer; treat with topical aciclovir.

mcq.q: How is primary genital herpes within 6 weeks of delivery managed?
o: Oral aciclovir plus elective caesarean section
mcq.r: **Oral aciclovir + elective caesarean**; intrapartum IV aciclovir if caesarean is declined.

o: Dorsal root ganglia of the thorax

technique.stem: A 22 year old woman has a 4 day history of painful vulval sores and burning on passing urine. She had tingling in the area for a day before they appeared. She has a new sexual partner. Examination shows multiple grouped vesicles and shallow ulcers on a red base on both labia, with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A genital lesion diagnosis: is it painful or painless, single or multiple?

clues: tingling in the area for a day
steps.x: Prodrome, painful grouped vesicles, dysuria, nodes, sexual risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Genital herpes**.

elim: Behçet's gives recurrent oral and genital ulcers with eye or skin disease, no vesicles.
Lichen sclerosus is itchy white plaques, not acute vesicles.
Syphilis gives a single painless chancre.
Candida causes itch and white discharge, not vesicles.

steps.x: **B. Genital herpes.** Painful + grouped vesicles + prodrome.

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman who is 36 weeks pregnant has a 2 day history of painful genital ulcers. She has never had genital sores before. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg. The obstetric team need the diagnosis confirmed to plan her delivery.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: HSV PCR on a lesion swab

steps.x: The test that **confirms** HSV, not a screening test.
Likely primary genital herpes near term: confirmation changes the birth plan.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **PCR (NAAT) on a lesion swab**.

elim: Serology helps decide primary versus recurrent but does not prove the ulcer is HSV.
Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary.
Syphilis serology is a useful screen, but syphilis ulcers are painless.
Urine culture does not detect HSV in ulcers.

steps.x: **A. HSV PCR on a lesion swab.** The most effective test.

technique.stem: A 26 year old woman who is 37 weeks pregnant has primary genital herpes confirmed by PCR, which started 1 week ago. She is taking oral aciclovir. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She has been offered an elective caesarean section but declines it and wishes to labour vaginally.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management when caesarean is declined.
Primary infection within 6 weeks of birth; she has capacity and declines surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Intrapartum IV aciclovir**.

elim: A capacitous woman can decline surgery; you cannot override her.
Induction does not reduce transmission.
Without treatment the neonatal risk is high.
Topical aciclovir gives no systemic protection.

steps.x: **C. Intrapartum IV aciclovir.** The alternative to caesarean.

technique.stem: A 19 year old man has a 2 day history of a cluster of painful blisters on his lower lip, which burst to form shallow ulcers. A skin sample shows the blisters lie within the epidermis, and the epidermal cells are swollen with multinucleated giant cells.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the blister formation?

steps.x: A mechanism question about vesicles.

clues: cluster of painful blisters on his lower lip
steps.x: Cold sore; intraepidermal blisters with viral cytopathic change.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HSV causes **keratinocyte ballooning degeneration**, forming intraepidermal blisters.

elim: Anti-desmoglein 3 is pemphigus vulgaris, not acute grouped lip vesicles.
Anti-hemidesmosome is bullous pemphigoid: tense subepidermal blisters in the elderly.
Staph toxin causes impetigo or scalded skin, with no giant cells.
Vasculitis causes purpura, not vesicles.

steps.x: **D. Ballooning degeneration.** Virus damages keratinocytes.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has a 3 day history of painful sores on his penis and burning when passing urine. He felt tingling before they appeared. His temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 88 bpm. He has had two new sexual partners this month. There are grouped shallow ulcers on a red base and tender inguinal lymph nodes.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Painful grouped ulcers after a tingling prodrome, with dysuria and tender nodes, is genital herpes. Syphilis is painless and single.

steps.x: Painful or painless genital ulcer?

clues: grouped shallow ulcers on a red base
steps.x: Classic HSV: prodrome, pain, grouping, dysuria, nodes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Genital herpes**.

elim: Chancroid gives a deep, ragged single ulcer, rare in the UK, without a vesicle stage.
Warts are painless growths.
Syphilis is a single painless chancre.
Scabies causes itchy burrows and papules.

steps.x: **B. Genital herpes.**

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman has tingling on her upper lip for a day, followed by a cluster of small painful blisters. She has had similar episodes after colds and sunny holidays. She is otherwise well. Her temperature is 37.0°C.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Recurrent cold sores triggered by illness and UV, with a tingling prodrome, are classically HSV-1 reactivating from the trigeminal ganglion.

steps.x: Organism for recurrent lip blisters.
Prodrome, grouped vesicles, triggers: illness and UV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HSV-1** reactivation.

elim: Coxsackie causes hand, foot and mouth in children, not recurrent lip sores.
EBV causes glandular fever.
HPV causes warts.
VZV gives a dermatomal rash, rarely recurrent on the lip.

steps.x: **C. HSV-1.** Classic cold sore.

practice.stem: A 41 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful red left eye, watering, sensitivity to light and blurred vision. He has a cold sore on his lip. He does not wear contact lenses. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. Fluorescein is applied to the eye.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on fluorescein staining?
practice.e: HSV keratitis gives a branching dendritic ulcer on fluorescein. A round ulcer suggests bacterial keratitis (contact lenses); linear scratches suggest a foreign body under the lid.

steps.x: Predict the fluorescein finding.
Painful red eye, photophobia, active HSV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dendritic ulcer** of HSV keratitis.

elim: Punctate staining fits dry eye, not HSV.
A round ulcer suggests bacterial keratitis, usually in lens wearers.
Corneal infection with pain and photophobia will stain.
Linear scratches suggest a foreign body under the lid.

steps.x: **A. Dendritic ulcer.**

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman has a 2 day history of a rash on her palms and the backs of her hands. The lesions are round with three concentric rings: a dark centre, a pale ring and a red outer ring. A week ago she had a cold sore. She takes no medicines. Her temperature is 37.2°C and pulse rate 80 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely trigger of her rash?
practice.e: Target lesions with three rings on the hands after a cold sore are erythema multiforme, most commonly triggered by HSV-1.

steps.x: What triggered the rash?

clues: palms and the backs of her hands
A week ago she had a cold sore
steps.x: Target lesions (erythema multiforme) after HSV; no drug trigger.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HSV-1**, the commonest trigger of erythema multiforme.

elim: She takes no medicines.
She takes no medicines; drugs trigger SJS more than EM.
Parvovirus causes slapped cheek.
Strep causes scarlet fever or erythema nodosum.

steps.x: **C. HSV-1.** Cold sore, then target lesions.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has a 3 day history of fever, headache and strange behaviour. Today he had a seizure. He is confused and smells odd things. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. MRI shows changes in the left temporal lobe.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, behaviour change, seizures, olfactory symptoms and temporal lobe changes with lymphocytic CSF and normal glucose are HSV encephalitis, a rare but severe complication.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an acute febrile brain illness.
Encephalitis (brain function change) localised to the temporal lobe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Herpes simplex encephalitis**.

elim: Bacterial meningitis gives neutrophils and low CSF glucose.
Migraine does not cause fever and CSF pleocytosis.
SAH is a sudden thunderclap headache.
A glioma is not acute with fever and CSF lymphocytes.

steps.x: **B. HSV encephalitis.** Temporal lobe + fever + confusion.

practice.stem: A 9 day old baby boy is lethargic and feeding poorly, with vesicles on his scalp and around his eye. He had a seizure this morning. His mother had painful genital ulcers for the first time at 38 weeks and delivered vaginally. His temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 182 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Skin, eye and mouth vesicles with encephalitis and sepsis after a vaginal birth to a mother with primary genital herpes within 6 weeks of delivery is neonatal HSV.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a sick neonate with vesicles.

clues: vesicles on his scalp and around his eye
painful genital ulcers for the first time at 38 weeks
steps.x: Primary maternal HSV within 6 weeks of birth, vaginal delivery, vesicles plus encephalitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Neonatal herpes simplex infection**.

elim: Erythema toxicum is a harmless rash in a well baby.
GBS sepsis does not cause vesicles; the maternal history points to HSV.
Impetigo gives honey-crusted lesions in a well child.
Varicella needs maternal chickenpox, not genital ulcers.

steps.x: **D. Neonatal HSV.** Maternal primary infection near term.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man with HIV has a 3 week history of painful perianal ulcers that are not typical in appearance. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Syphilis serology is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: HSV PCR (NAAT) on a lesion swab
practice.e: PCR (NAAT) on a lesion swab is the most effective test and supports the diagnosis in atypical or recurrent presentations, common when immunosuppressed.

steps.x: Confirmatory test for an atypical ulcer.
Immunosuppressed, painful, atypical: HSV likely, needs confirming.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HSV PCR on a lesion swab**.

elim: Dark-ground microscopy is for syphilis, already negative.
IgG shows past infection, not the cause of this ulcer.
Biopsy is second-line if PCR is negative.
Urine microscopy will not diagnose an ulcer.

steps.x: **C. HSV PCR.** Gold standard on a lesion swab.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman sees her GP with tingling on her lower lip followed by a cluster of painful vesicles on a red base. She has had identical episodes twice a year for 10 years. She is otherwise well, and the lesions look classic.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: HSV is usually diagnosed clinically from characteristic grouped vesicles. PCR on a swab is reserved for ambiguous or atypical lesions.

steps.x: Initial investigation for a typical cold sore.

clues: cluster of painful vesicles on a red base
steps.x: Classic recurrent HSV-1.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clinical diagnosis**, no test.

elim: A bacterial swab looks for the wrong organism.
Serology does not diagnose an episode.
Biopsy is never needed for a classic cold sore.
Blood PCR is for systemic disease such as neonatal HSV.

steps.x: **D. Clinical diagnosis.** Swab only if atypical.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has her first episode of genital herpes, with painful vulval ulcers and dysuria for 2 days. She is not pregnant and has no allergies. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. She is passing urine.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Aciclovir 400 mg oral three times daily for 5 days
Aciclovir IV 10 mg/kg three times daily
practice.e: First-line treatment is oral aciclovir 400 mg TDS for 5 days, with analgesia, hygiene and abstinence until healed. IV aciclovir is for encephalitis or neonatal infection.

steps.x: First-line treatment for genital herpes.
Uncomplicated, not pregnant, no retention: outpatient treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral aciclovir 400 mg TDS for 5 days**.

elim: IV is for severe disease such as encephalitis.
Penicillin treats syphilis.
Ceftriaxone treats gonorrhoea.
Steroids do not treat a virus.

steps.x: **A. Oral aciclovir.**

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman who is 36 weeks pregnant has a 3 day history of painful genital ulcers. PCR confirms HSV-2, and serology shows this is a primary infection. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. She wants to do what is safest for her baby.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Elective caesarean section with oral aciclovir
IV aciclovir for the baby only after birth
Planned vaginal delivery with no treatment
practice.e: Primary genital herpes within 6 weeks of delivery: oral aciclovir plus elective caesarean, which avoids contact with infected genital secretions in the birth canal.

steps.x: Delivery plan for HSV in late pregnancy.
Primary episode within 6 weeks of delivery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral aciclovir + elective caesarean**.

elim: Induction still means vaginal delivery through infected secretions.
Waiting until after birth misses prevention.
Highest risk of neonatal herpes.
Topical treatment does not protect the baby.

steps.x: **A. Elective caesarean with oral aciclovir.**

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has a painful, red, watering right eye with photophobia for 2 days. She had a cold sore last week. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. Fluorescein staining shows a branching dendritic ulcer on the cornea.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Herpes simplex keratitis is treated first-line with topical aciclovir. Topical steroids such as dexamethasone can worsen the ulcer.

steps.x: First-line treatment for HSV keratitis.
Dendritic ulcer = HSV keratitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Topical aciclovir**; no steroids.

elim: Steroids worsen HSV keratitis.
Chloramphenicol is antibacterial and will not treat HSV.
Topical steroids can make the ulcer much worse.
An NSAID drop does not treat the virus.

steps.x: **B. Topical aciclovir.** Never steroids on a dendritic ulcer.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has recurrent cold sores on the same part of her upper lip two or three times a year, usually after a cold or sunbathing. Each episode starts with tingling at the site. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Where does the virus most likely lie latent between episodes?
practice.e: HSV-1 establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion and travels back down the nerve when reactivated by illness, stress or UV, causing recurrences at the same site.

steps.x: Site of HSV-1 latency.

clues: same part of her upper lip
steps.x: Same-site recurrences after triggers: reactivation from a sensory ganglion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Trigeminal ganglion**.

elim: T4 dorsal root ganglion is a VZV shingles site, not the lip.
Geniculate ganglion is linked with Ramsay Hunt (VZV).
Sacral ganglia are the site for genital HSV-2.
Latency is in neurons, not skin cells.

steps.x: **E. Trigeminal ganglion.**

prompts.q: What is HSV, and which types cause which disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: classic site for each type, then the caveat.

points.p: Viral infection causing painful vesicular lesions on skin or mucosa
HSV-1: classically oral herpes (cold sores)
HSV-2: classically genital herpes
Either type can cause disease at either site
points.why: Oral sex spreads HSV-1 to the genitals.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the order of events.

points.p: Burning or tingling prodrome
Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Rupture into painful ulcers
Local lymphadenopathy and dysuria

prompts.q: What triggers recurrence, and what advice is given about sex?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: reactivation of latent virus.

points.p: Stress or intercurrent illness
Immunosuppression and UV exposure
Abstain from sex until prodrome and lesions fully resolve

prompts.q: How does HSV keratitis present and what does fluorescein show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: painful red eye plus one stain finding.

points.p: Painful red eye
Photophobia, foreign body sensation, blurred vision
Dendritic ulcer on fluorescein staining

prompts.q: What is erythema multiforme and how is it linked to HSV?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the lesion and the trigger.

points.p: Target lesions with three concentric rings
Typically on the hands and feet
Most commonly triggered by HSV-1

prompts.q: What is neonatal herpes, how is it caught, and what other severe complication should you know?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: timing of maternal infection.

points.p: Vesicles on skin, eye or mouth with encephalitis and sepsis
Transmitted during delivery if mother has primary infection within 6 weeks of birth

prompts.q: How is HSV diagnosed, and what is the gold standard test?

points.p: Usually clinical, from characteristic grouped vesicles
NAAT/PCR on a lesion swab is most effective
points.why: Swab the base of an ulcer.

points.p: PCR supports diagnosis in ambiguous or recurrent presentations
points.why: Also used in pregnancy and immunosuppression.

prompts.q: What is the first-line treatment for oral or genital herpes, with dose and alternatives?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: drug, dose, frequency, duration.

points.p: Oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days
Valaciclovir or famciclovir as alternatives

prompts.q: How do you manage HSV keratitis and primary genital herpes near delivery?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one drug to give, one to avoid, one operation.

points.p: Keratitis: topical aciclovir
Avoid topical steroids
Primary genital herpes within 6 weeks of delivery: oral aciclovir plus elective caesarean

prompts.q: Why does HSV recur, and where does it hide?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: virus type, site of latency, route back.

points.p: Double-stranded DNA virus that becomes latent in sensory nerve ganglia
HSV-1: trigeminal ganglion; HSV-2: sacral ganglia
Reactivation travels back down the nerve to cause recurrent lesions

prompts.q: Why do vesicles form, why does encephalitis hit the temporal lobes, and why does caesarean protect?

points.p: Keratinocyte ballooning degeneration causes intraepidermal blisters that rupture to ulcers
Encephalitis spreads along olfactory or trigeminal tracts to the temporal lobes

Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction to HSV antigens
points.why: Not active infection of the skin lesions.

glossary.HSV: Herpes simplex virus: a double-stranded DNA virus causing painful vesicles; types 1 and 2.
glossary.HSV-1: Herpes simplex virus type 1: classically causes cold sores; latent in the trigeminal ganglion.
glossary.HSV-2: Herpes simplex virus type 2: classically causes genital herpes; latent in the sacral ganglia.
glossary.Cold sore: Recurrent HSV blisters on or around the lip.
glossary.Prodrome: Early warning symptoms, such as tingling or burning, before lesions appear.
glossary.Dysuria: Pain or burning on passing urine.
glossary.Latency: A dormant state in which the virus persists in nerve cells without causing disease.
glossary.Reactivation: Latent virus becoming active again and causing a recurrence.
glossary.Trigeminal ganglion: Sensory nerve cluster of cranial nerve V; site of HSV-1 latency.
glossary.Sacral ganglia: Sensory nerve clusters at the base of the spine; site of HSV-2 latency.
glossary.Primary infection: The first-ever infection with HSV, with no existing antibodies; usually the most severe.
glossary.NAAT: Nucleic acid amplification test, such as PCR, that detects viral DNA.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction: amplifies viral DNA from a swab to confirm and type HSV.
glossary.Aciclovir: Antiviral that blocks herpes DNA replication; 400 mg TDS for 5 days for oral or genital herpes.
glossary.Valaciclovir: Prodrug of aciclovir with better absorption, so fewer daily doses.
glossary.Famciclovir: Alternative oral antiviral for herpes infections.
glossary.Herpes simplex keratitis: HSV infection of the cornea causing a painful red eye and a dendritic ulcer.
glossary.Dendritic ulcer: Branching corneal ulcer seen with fluorescein; the sign of HSV keratitis.
glossary.Fluorescein: Orange dye that stains damaged cornea green under blue light.
glossary.Photophobia: Pain or discomfort on exposure to light.
glossary.Erythema multiforme: Hypersensitivity rash with target lesions on the hands and feet, most often triggered by HSV-1.
glossary.Target lesion: Round skin lesion with three concentric rings: dark centre, pale ring, red outer ring.
glossary.Neonatal herpes: HSV infection of a newborn caught during delivery; can cause encephalitis and sepsis.
glossary.Herpes encephalitis: HSV infection of the brain, typically the temporal lobes; causes fever, confusion and seizures.
glossary.Encephalitis: Inflammation of the brain tissue, causing altered behaviour, confusion or seizures.
glossary.Temporal lobe: Part of the brain involved in memory, smell and behaviour; targeted by HSV encephalitis.
glossary.Elective caesarean section: A planned surgical delivery before labour starts.
glossary.Ballooning degeneration: Swelling and breakdown of virus-infected keratinocytes that splits the epidermis into blisters.
glossary.Keratinocyte: The main cell of the epidermis.
glossary.Primary syphilis: Treponema pallidum infection causing a single painless genital ulcer (chancre).
glossary.BASHH: British Association for Sexual Health and HIV, which writes UK sexual health guidelines.
glossary.Multinucleated giant cells: Fused infected cells with several nuclei, seen in herpes virus infections.
